lead: Both readings are about wealth and what it can and cannot buy. Paul tells Timothy what to say to the rich: do not be haughty, do not hope in riches, be rich in good works, and so “take hold of the life that really is life”. In Matthew, after the rich young man has gone away sad, Jesus says that it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom, and then adds that for God all things are possible. The key words are hope, deposit and hundredfold.

r.h: The life that really is life
set: After the solemn doxology of vv. 15–16 the letter returns to practical matters. Ephesus was a rich commercial city, and the church there included people of means. Earlier in the chapter the letter warned those who want to be rich (6:9–10); now it speaks to those who already are.
The last verses go back to the letter's first concern: false teaching (1:3–7). Timothy is to guard what he has received and avoid empty talk.
str: vv. 17–19: a charge to the rich: hope in God, do good, share, and so lay up a good foundation.
vv. 20–21a: guard the deposit; avoid what is falsely called knowledge.
kw: the life that really is life
Riches give a life that looks like life. The letter points to the life that is real, the life of God which begins now and lasts.
From the same root as koinōnia, communion. Sharing goods is the outward side of sharing in the one life of Christ.
what has been entrusted, the deposit
A legal word for something left in another's safekeeping, to be returned intact. The Catechism uses this text for the deposit of faith entrusted by the apostles to the whole Church (CCC 84).
vv: As for those who in the present age are rich, command them not to be haughty, or to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but rather on God who richly provides us with everything for our enjoyment.
The letter does not condemn the good things of creation; God gives them “for our enjoyment”. The danger lies in pride and in false hope.
so that they may take hold of the life that really is life.
Timothy, guard what has been entrusted to you.

The phrase “what is falsely called knowledge” (in Greek, pseudōnymos gnōsis) gave St Irenaeus the title of his great work against the Gnostics, the “Refutation and Overthrow of Knowledge Falsely So Called”.
ch: The Church teaches the universal destination of goods: what we own is given to us also for others (CCC 2402–2406). Generosity is one way of laying up treasure in heaven, as the Lord said (Matthew 6:20), and it is done by grace, not to buy grace. The command to guard the deposit stands behind the Church's care to hand on the faith whole, the faith which the apostles received from the Lord and which the Holy Spirit keeps alive in her (CCC 84).

r.h: For God all things are possible
set: A rich young man has just asked Jesus what good deed he must do to have eternal life. Told to sell his possessions and follow, he went away grieving, “for he had many possessions” (19:22). Jesus now turns to his disciples.
In the thinking of the time, riches were often taken as a sign of God's blessing (compare Deuteronomy 28:1–14). That is why the disciples are so astounded: if the blessed cannot be saved, who can?
str: vv. 23–24: the hardness of entering the kingdom for the rich; the camel and the needle.
vv. 25–26: “Who can be saved?” “For God all things are possible.”
v. 27: Peter's question: what will we have?
vv. 28–29: the reward of the Twelve and of all who leave everything.
v. 30: the first and the last.
kw: The largest animal in Palestine and the smallest opening anyone knew: a deliberate picture of the impossible. The popular story of a small city gate called “the needle's eye” has no ancient evidence behind it. A few late manuscripts read kamilos, “rope”, which shows that some readers found the saying too hard.
Literally “new birth”. It is used here of the renewal of the world at the end, and in Titus 3:5 of baptism. Both meanings belong together: the new creation begins in the font.
An overflowing return. Mark adds that it comes “with persecutions” (Mark 10:30).
vv: it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for someone who is rich to enter the kingdom of God.
For mortals it is impossible, but for God all things are possible.
Jesus does not soften his saying; he points beyond human strength. The same truth was spoken to Abraham (Genesis 18:14) and to the Virgin Mary at the Annunciation (Luke 1:37).
everyone who has left houses or brothers or sisters or father or mother or children or fields, for my name’s sake, will receive a hundredfold, and will inherit eternal life.
“For my name's sake” is the key. Loss for its own sake is not the point; love of the Lord is.
ch: Clement of Alexandria, in his little book Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?, taught that the Lord asks us to banish from the soul the passion for wealth more than wealth itself, and to use what we have for others (in substance). The Catechism speaks of poverty of heart: Jesus asks his disciples to prefer him to everything and everyone (CCC 2544–2547). Every vocation that leaves home and fields for the Lord, the priest's, the religious sister's or brother's and the missionary's, lives from this promise.

qa: Is it wrong to be rich?

No. Abraham and Job were rich, and the letter to Timothy speaks of God who gives us everything “for our enjoyment”. The danger is to trust in riches, to be proud because of them, and to keep them from those in need. What is impossible for us, a heart loosened from that grip, God can give.
study: Where do I set my hope: on what I have, or on God who gives it?
What has the Lord asked me to leave for his name's sake, and what “hundredfold” have I already received?
